en: Commentary on the Three Maitreya Sūtras;
Record of the Collation of the Maitreya’s Descent from Above Sūtra; Record of the Collation of the Maitreya’s Descent from Above Sūtra.
In order to explain this sutra, it shall be analyzed briefly by means of five sections:
first, an account of the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching; second, a detailed differentiation of [the subject matter]... [and so forth]. [The remaining sections follow.]
□□□□□. Fifth is the word-by-word commentary.
Regarding what is called □□□□□, there are two parts:
first, a brief exposition; second, a detailed exposition.

Regarding this brief exposition: I humbly consider that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is profoundly deep; its essence pervades the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), and its function encompasses the universe. Because its essence pervades the dharma-realm, it is difficult to measure its distance or proximity; because its function encompasses the universe, how could emptiness and existence ever be fathomed?
The ultimate truth and phenomena are identical, yet there is nothing to be fused;
wisdom realizes the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Because there is nothing to be illuminated, there is nothing that is not illuminated; because there is nothing to be fused, there is nothing that is not fused.

Because there is nothing that is not harmonized, the mirror of the single mind manifests both principle and phenomena; because there is nothing that is not illuminated, the mirror-like wisdom (ādarśa-jñāna) is submerged within the ocean of suchness (tathatā). This meaning is fully realized and thoroughly verified by the perfect wisdom of the Supreme Sage.
Therefore, the Great Being Maitreya has ascended to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (Miaojue) while manifesting his traces within the Sahā world.
Because he has ascended to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment, the darkness of the two obstacles is reflected and dispelled by the mirror of the four wisdoms.
His traces were left in the Sahā world, [bestowing] such-and-such virtues.
Therefore, because his virtue is lofty, the various māras naturally crumble;
because his merit is great, the various heterodox schools submit like this.
Thus, the path is opened and the gate of nirvāṇa is revealed.

In order to bring rest to the wheel of suffering, [the Buddha] dwells nearby in Tuṣita and, in the distant future, will appear at the time of the kalpa’s destruction; because [he is] named [so-and-so], he preaches this sutra.

Regarding the second point, the detailed analysis: for the time being, [the practitioner] generates a mind of reverence through the pure faith of realization (*avetyaprasāda*) regarding the Noble Ones and the sublime Dharma.
Second, it is to engender a mind of reverence for the True Dharma, so as to manifest what has been heard and inspire faith.
Third, it is out of a desire to assemble the multitude; by emitting light to summon them, they gather like clouds upon seeing the signs.
Fourth, it is because when he is about to preach the Dharma, flowers rain down and the earth trembles in order to introduce the narrative.
Fifth, it is because he wishes to proclaim the true meaning and perform many deeds.

The "true meaning" (tattvārtha) refers to the authentic core of all the sūtras; because it brings benefit and happiness in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings, it is called the true meaning.
"Meaning" (artha) here signifies "beneficial purpose" (artha-lābha).

Regarding "performing much" (*bahukara*): because it rescues and delivers beings in the final age to an infinite degree based on the previously established true meaning, it is called "performing much.

Although "performing much" should logically constitute the sixth [category], because it conveys the true meaning to those whose faculties are ready for deliverance, it is combined with the preceding and judged as one.
Regarding these marks, they must be required by the great [beings] until the end.
To proclaim the causes and conditions, they are briefly summarized into three meanings:
first, that which is produced through spiritual power, namely the gathering of the various honored ones and the various [beings]. Second... [text missing].
The two kinds of activity of wisdom consist of the speaker and the true meaning;
the three kinds of activity of compassion consist of [the benefit of] many [sentient beings].
Regarding these five characteristics as a standard: the *Sūtra on the Descent from the Tuṣita Heaven* (*Upapatti-sūtra*) fully possesses those five characteristics;
the *Sūtra on the Birth in the World* (*Jāti-sūtra*) lacks the two characteristics of "gathering the assembly" and "narrating the events";
and the *Sūtra on the Buddha’s Life* (*Buddhacarita-sūtra*) possesses only the first and last two characteristics.
The reason for this is that the Tathāgata’s skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) are not [limited to] a single mode.
Although there are differences in the characteristics of those who may be transformed, he nonetheless teaches the sūtras according to two types of recipients:
first, the noble ones (*ārya*); second, ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).
The first part further has two [sections]:

the first is for the sake of the bodhisattvas of this land, as the sutra says: "When the Tathāgata speaks with a single voice, he expounds ten billion dharanī-gates, and Maitreya Bodhisattva attains them immediately at that very moment."

Second is the transformation of bodhisattvas from other directions, as the sutra says: "The Tathāgata speaks of the ten wholesome karmas and their retributions in Tuṣita Heaven; the bodhisattvas of the ten directions thereby attain the dharma-gate of the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."
Subsequently, there are three grades among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*).

Those who practice at the superior level may either cultivate the Buddha-contemplation samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*) or repent of their various transgressions; they shall behold Maitreya in this very body. Regarding the differences in their spiritual excellence and the dimensions of the forms they perceive, these are explained in detail in the *Vaipulya-dhāraṇī Sūtra* and the *Sūtra on the Ascent [to Tuṣita]*.

As for those who practice at the intermediate level, they may cultivate the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha or cultivate pure karma; after casting off their bodies, they will be reborn in that heaven, where they will eventually reach the stage of non-retrogression upon meeting Maitreya, just as described in the *Sūtra on the Upper Rebirth*.
As for those of inferior practice, they cultivate various virtues such as giving and precepts, and give rise to great vows to meet Maitreya.

After casting off this body, they will be reborn according to their karma until the time Maitreya attains enlightenment, at which point they shall encounter him and be delivered during his three assemblies; this is precisely as described in the two sūtras, the *Sutra on the Descent* and the *Sutra on Attaining Buddhahood*.
Some say that the *Sūtra on the Ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven* is intended to transform those of middle capacity, while the other two sūtras are intended to transform those of lower capacity;
as for those of superior capacity, they are precisely the objects of the Mahāvaipulya (Vaipulya) sūtras.

Regarding the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realm*, if one categorizes the two middle sections as the "Upper Section" yet does not treat them as such, this would contradict the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realm*, for it states: "At the time of death, Maitreya will emit the light of the marks of a Great Man to welcome this person."
Therefore, the former [position] is superior.
Question:
Although the eight phases differ, they constitute but a single continuous body belonging to Maitreya.
Since the body is not different, why does the Tathāgata separately preach three sutras?
Answer:
It is truly because the capacities and awakenings of sentient beings differ.
What are the differences?
Briefly, there are fourteen kinds.

First, for the sake of causing sentient beings who have not yet planted roots of goodness to plant them, he preached the *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Upper Realms*; for those who have already planted roots of goodness so that they may attain liberation, he preached the other two sūtras.

Second, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* is taught because it describes the cultivation of great causes for all sentient beings, while the other two sūtras are taught to show that sentient beings can attain minor fruits.

Third, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* is taught so that sentient beings may gain benefit from hearing praises of the bodhisattva’s merits, while the other two sūtras are taught so that sentient beings may gain benefit from hearing praises of attaining buddhahood.

Fourth, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* was taught so that sentient beings might plant various roots of goodness and obtain benefits; the other two sūtras were taught so that sentient beings might plant roots of goodness over a long period and thereby obtain benefits.
Fifth, he preached the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* so that sentient beings might see the Buddha from afar; he preached the other two sūtras so that sentient beings might see the Buddha nearby.

Sixth, he preached the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* so that sentient beings might obtain benefit in Tuṣita Heaven; he preached the other two sūtras so that sentient beings might obtain benefit in Jambudvīpa.

Seventh, because sentient beings hear [of the celestial palaces] and pray to be reborn in those heavenly mansions, he preached the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above*; and in order to cause sentient beings to see that the jeweled pavilions are subject to destruction and thus realize their non-substantiality, he preached the other two sūtras.

Eighth, because sentient beings derive benefit from seeing many bodies of the Buddha, the *Sūtra on the Ascent to the Heavens* was taught; because sentient beings derive benefit from seeing the body of a single Buddha, the other two sūtras were taught.

Ninth, because sentient beings receive benefit through his body in the Tuṣita Heaven, he preached the *Sūtra on the Ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven*; because they receive benefit by renouncing the world in Jambudvīpa, he preached the other two sūtras.

Tenth, because sentient beings gain benefit by hearing Śākyamuni praise Maitreya, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* was taught; and because sentient beings gain benefit by hearing Maitreya praise Śākyamuni, the other two sūtras were taught.

Eleventh, because sentient beings gain benefit upon hearing the first of Maitreya’s thirty-two marks, the *Sūtra on Rebirth Above* was taught; and because sentient beings gain benefit upon hearing the latter seven marks, the other two sūtras were taught.

The *Sūtra on Rebirth in the Higher Realms* was taught because twelve [beings] were to hear it through the request of Upagupta, thereby attaining benefit; the other two sūtras were taught so that sentient beings would hear them through the requests of Śāriputra and Aśvajit, thereby attaining benefit.
Thirteenth, three sūtras are taught so that one may know the distinctions between superior and inferior excellence regarding the fruits of birth in higher and lower realms.

Fourteenth, three sūtras are taught so that one may know the differences in the magnitude of the causes and effects of the two types of primary retribution (the physical body) in higher and lower realms.
Second, regarding the essence of the teaching, there are two parts:
first, a general exposition of the essence of the school; second, a specific exposition of the essence of the school.
As for the "general exposition," this refers to the teachings of the two schools.

This refers to the frequent assertion made by various masters of the region south of the Yangtze River that the essence of a thesis (*pakṣa*) is established by way of its expressed meaning; they state that the thesis is the essence and the essence is the thesis, because there is no distinction between the thesis and its essence.
The masters of the present Tang era say:
"The teaching is called the *sūtra*, while the meaning is called the *śāstra* (or *zong*); therefore, the substance of the *śāstra* differs [from that of the *sūtra*].
This explanation contains both merits and defects.
That is to say, if it were as stated previously, the objects of the two types of unimpeded knowledge—dharma and meaning—would have to be identical.
For the treatise states: "The unimpeded knowledge of dharmas takes names and so forth as its object;
the unimpeded knowledge of meaning takes that which is signified as its object."
If it were as stated in the latter [interpretation], the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the sūtra would not constitute its meaning.
If that were the case, it would contradict both the treatise and its intended meaning.

This is because the former meaning serves as the gateway for generating understanding within the meaning itself, while the latter meaning serves as the gateway for differentiating within the teaching and the meaning; thus, it is also termed "attained in common."
Thus, in discerning the nature and substance of the teachings, there are naturally two approaches:
first, the distinction between the teaching and its meaning, wherein the substance and the tenet differ; that is, "teaching" refers to the substance, while "meaning" refers to the tenet.
The second is the gate of identical function between word and meaning, wherein the essence of the thesis (*pakṣa*) is no different.
This means that the meaning is also the teaching, and the teaching is also the meaning, because the essence of the thesis is no different [from them].
As the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "That which is the object-condition (*ālambana*) of phenomena refers to the sets of names, phrases, and phonemes," for the thesis is identical to their essence.

The *Jiuzhong* [Commentary] states: "The 'manifestation of the essence' (*xiantti*) refers to the ten meanings that are the objects of exposition. Here, "essence" (*ti*) refers to the thesis (*zong*), for the *Fajieguan* states: "The essence of the sūtra is twofold:
first, the letter; second, the meaning."
Next, to specifically clarify the central tenet of the sutra, there are three explanations.
The first states:
This sutra takes samādhi as its central tenet; that is to say, because the aspiration to be born in Tuṣita and to behold Maitreya cannot be accomplished unless one possesses samādhi.
One says: Not so.

For even if one cultivates meditative concentration (*samādhi*), if there is no contemplative mind (*vipaśyanā-citta*), nothing at all will be accomplished; therefore, it should be said that the contemplative mind is the primary tenet.
Therefore, the subsequent passage of the sutra states: "If one contemplates in this way, it is called right contemplation; if one contemplates otherwise, it is called wrong contemplation.
Furthermore, if this were not accepted, it would contradict the title of the work, which concerns the meaning of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*).
One school says:

What was stated previously is not entirely consistent with reason, because it is certain that [the object] is not the cause of the desire realm, and because contemplation is not its primary objective; therefore, one should state that the thesis consists precisely in the causes and effects upon which [the practice] relies.
The latter explanation is considered superior, yet three interpretations are presented herein.

One states that the thesis consists solely in the cause and effect of sentient beings being born in heaven and seeing the Noble Ones; that is to say, humans are born in heaven and the gods attain non-retrogression, as this constitutes the general purport of the sutra.
One says:
This is precisely to manifest that Maitreya’s birth in Tuṣita is for the benefit of sentient beings, as this accords with the intended meaning of the sūtra text.
Another says:

It takes as its primary tenet the causes and effects—both primary and secondary—of both bodhisattvas and sentient beings. Thus, when the Sūtra states, "This is called the Tushita Heaven, the place of supreme and wondrous merit that is the retribution for the ten wholesome actions," it is precisely revealing the causes and effects of the bodhisattva.
Furthermore, the later passage stating that "the Buddha’s disciples who practice the six [perfections] are immediately born in that heaven" reveals the cause and effect of sentient beings.

However, in the title, the phrase "contemplating the cause of sentient beings" and the word "birth" (which indicates the fruit of the Bodhisattva) are used as mutual illustrations through elliptical abbreviation.
Having already clarified the essential tenets of the *Sūtra on the Upper Rebirth*, we now proceed to clarify the essential tenets of the two sūtras. Regarding this, there are two interpretations:

first, some say that the *Sūtra on the Lower Rebirth* is taken as the primary tenet because it extensively explains the primary and secondary retributions (*āśraya-vipāka* and *sambhoga-vipāka*) as well as the causes for cultivation to achieve rebirth in the desire realm.

The *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* (*Chengfo jing*) takes as its primary tenet the extensive manifestation of the buddha-fields and the divine virtues of the Buddha, as well as the causes and conditions by which sentient beings perceive the Buddha.

Now, it is said that this is not so, because both sūtras are identical regarding the two types of retribution—the primary and the secondary—as well as the manner in which sentient beings perceive the Buddha.

It should be said that both sutras teach sentient beings through the seven marks of Maitreya; according to their respective capacities, they take as their primary tenet the attainment of the fruit of self-abandonment.

Third, regarding the single and multiple versions of the sutra: herein, we first distinguish between the single and multiple versions, and subsequently distinguish between the authentic and the spurious.
Regarding the single and the double [versions]: the eight-folio *Sūtra on the Upper Birth* was translated by Zhu Foshuo of Anyanghou during the Northern Liang dynasty.
The nine-folio *Sūtra on the Lower Birth* was translated by Kumārajīva at Baoyin Temple in Yuzhang in the third year of the Chengsheng era of the Jin dynasty.
The seventeen-fascicle *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* was translated by Dharmarakṣa of the Western Jin dynasty.
Later, during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin, Kumārajīva translated the six-fascicle *Avalokita-sūtra*, which is titled "Maitreya’s Prophecy."

Furthermore, there is a separate translation titled *The Sūtra on Maitreya’s Time of Accomplishment*, which consists of three sheets; however, as its wording is incomplete, the former version has been retained.

These—the seventeen-sheet *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood*, the six-sheets [of the] *Sūtra on the Descent*, and the three-sheet *Sūtra on the Time of Accomplishment*—were translated in the fourth year of Hongshi and constitute the second edition.

The *Song lu* states: "The *Sutra on Becoming a Buddha in Seventeen Sheets*, the *Sutra on the Future Descent in Six Sheets*, and the *Sutra on the Time of Accomplishment in Three Sheets* are different translations of the same original text."
However, it does not mention the *Hongshi jing*.
These [versions] of seventeen sheets, six sheets, and three sheets are largely identical with minor differences to the translation by Dharmarakṣa;
this is seen in the *Erqin lu*.
The *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* translated by the śramaṇa Daobiao of Chang’an is the third translation.
During the Qi dynasty, the śramaṇa Daozheng further abridged it from beginning to end, naming it the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood*, also known as the *Sūtra on the Descent [of Maitreya]*.
Furthermore, at the beginning of this sutra is Mahāprajñā Śāriputra.
Master Ji said:
"The *Sutra on the Descent into the World* exists in two versions."
The "Large" version contains the phrase "Thus have I heard," translated during the Jin dynasty by Dharmarakṣa;
the "Small" version contains the phrase "The Great Wisdom Śāriputra," translated during the Jin dynasty by Kumārajīva.
The ancients said that there are differences in the translations of the *Puruṣa* (the person). Master Ji said:
"The 'Great' [Sūtra] consists of three parts; however, the absence of a *Nidāna* (Introductory Section) is merely due to the brevity of the verses."

In summary, the first is the single-text version, while the latter two are the expanded versions; this is because the *Sūtra on the Descent* was translated twice and the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* was translated three times.
Regarding the subsequent examination of authenticity and falsity: these three sutras are all authentic and not spurious.
This concludes the analysis of the third section.
However, setting aside the current topic, we shall now further discuss a related point as it arises from the discussion.
Question:
Are these three sūtras subsumed under the Mahāyāna or are they teachings of the Hīnayāna?
Answer:
There are three interpretations. One says:
Since these three sūtras all originate from the Āgamas, they are all subsumed under the Hīnayāna.
If it were not so, it would contradict such meanings as "possessing the body of an ordinary person" and "not yet having severed the various outflows.

One school of thought maintains that the *Sūtra on the Ascent to the Tuṣita Heaven* is subsumed within the Mahāyāna, because the sūtra states: "Within the halo surrounding his body, there is the Śūraṅgama Samādhi."

The other two sutras are both subsumed under the Hīnayāna; that is to say, the *Sūtra on the Descent* is derived from the *Ekottarika Āgama*, and the *Sūtra on Attaining Buddhahood* is derived from the *Dīrgha Āgama*. This is because their textual meaning is shallow and they result in only the fruits of the Lesser Vehicle.
One school of thought says:

The previous explanations have not fully exhausted the principle, for all three sūtras contain both Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna variations. Specifically, in the *Sūtra on the Ascent to Tuṣita*, it is first stated that for the sake of Bhadrapāla, Mañjuśrī, and others, one may also constantly practice the conduct of non-retrogression during the six periods; thus, five hundred billion devas and humans do not retrogress from unexcelled enlightenment.
Upāli occupies a subordinate position and his understanding is limited; thus, he poses this question using the framework of an ordinary person's body and so forth.

The *Sūtra on the Descent [of Maitreya]* distinguishes the qualities of permanence and so forth, as well as the meanings of permanence and so forth, in a manner identical to the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*.

Furthermore, the *Ekottarika Āgama* was translated by Dharmanandi during the Jianyuan era of the Former Qin, and the *Sūtra on the Descent [of Maitreya]* was translated by Kumārajīva during the Hongshi era of the Later Qin; therefore, it is absolutely impossible for these to have been extracted from the *Ekottarika Āgama*.

Furthermore, the *Mahāsambodhi-sūtra* states: "In all three assemblies where the Dharma was preached, [all] attained the fruits of the two vehicles and resolved to attain unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. For this reason, the assembly of bodhisattvas is omitted here.
Therefore, one should know that all three sutras undoubtedly embody the principle of the Mahayana.
Question:
What is the meaning of "sudden" and "gradual"?
Answer:
There are two explanations. One says:

The *Sūtra on the Rebirth in the Upper Realm* is subsumed under the Sudden Teaching, because its inconceivable dhāraṇīs, the Śūraṅgama Samādhi, and so forth, are not attainable by those of the Two Vehicles.
One interpretation states:
"This sutra is subsumed under the gradual teaching (*anupūrvika-yāna*), because humans, devas, and the eight classes of beings vow to be reborn in those heavens.
However, for now, the latter explanation is considered superior, because all the bhikṣus and others receive its transformative benefit.
The meaning of the other two sutras may be understood in the same way.
Fourth, regarding the explanation of the title, there are three parts:
first, a general discussion of the name; second, a specific explanation of the title; and third, a comprehensive interpretation of the title.
This is the first [point].
According to the subsequent sections of the sutra, it has two titles:
the first is the *Maitreya-parinirvāṇa-sūtra*, and the second is the *Sūtra on Contemplating Bodhisattva Maitreya’s Rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven and Arousing the Bodhicitta*.
Some say:
Although the title at the beginning of the sutra applies to both names, neither is fully comprehensive. Why is this?
Although the first title mentions the name of Maitreya Bodhisattva, it lacks the term *parinirvāṇa*;
although the latter title establishes the observation of Tuṣita Heaven, it briefly addresses the arousal of the bodhicitta.

Some say that the first name is the name by which Maitreya Bodhisattva passed away, while the latter name is the name by which Maitreya Bodhisattva was reborn in heaven; therefore, the title of this sutra is established using that second name.

The reason for this is that within the "Main Body" (*mūla-bhāga*) of the sutra, the birth and death of Maitreya and his rebirth in heaven are fully explained, while in its "Subsequent Section" (*uttara-bhāga*), both names are listed in detail.
Therefore, the Upādhyāya said:
"Both interpretations fail to exhaust the principle, because it is not necessarily the Buddha’s own teaching that established the titles of the sutra and the chapters."
Therefore, one should state that this sutra has three titles, as the initial title has been added to the two preceding sutras.
That is to say, the first was established by a sutra compiler, while the latter two were spoken by the Tathāgata.
For this reason, the meaning of the title differs from that of the latter two names.
Second, regarding the specific explanation of the title: the phrase "The Buddha says there is" proclaims the speaker, the Master.

Regarding the statement "contemplating Maitreya Bodhisattva’s rebirth in the Tuṣita Heaven," this expresses both the subject who contemplates and the object of contemplation; that is, it causes sentient beings to cultivate the causal practices.
However, because the expression is abbreviated, it simply says "contemplating."
As for the term "sūtra," it refers to the *Kṣānti-sūtra* (Discourse on Accordance).
As for the term "Buddha," in its full Sanskrit form it may be called *Buddha*, which here means "the Awakened One.
The "Buddha" mentioned here refers to both the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation body) and the *saṃbhogakāya* (enjoyment body).
Regarding "discourse" (*vyavahāra*), it is defined by the negation of "possessing words"; this is the converse statement, meaning that the phonemes and meanings are capable of arising.
In this context, some say:
through the sovereign power of the Tathāgata’s compassion and original vows, the appearances of phonemes and meanings manifest upon the consciousness of the listener.
Although the meaning of these words arises directly from the power of one’s own roots of goodness, they are called "the Buddha's teaching" by virtue of their dominant conditions. Some say:
due to the superior power of the listener’s roots of goodness, the aspects of word and meaning arise within the consciousness of the Tathāgata.
The characteristics of the meaning of this text arise from the Buddha’s roots of goodness for the benefit of others; therefore, it is called "the Buddha's teaching.
Hereafter, the explanation of the "supreme" is given, because the state of Buddhahood is fully endowed with both material and mental qualities.

Therefore, upon the eighth consciousness of the Tathāgata, the causal and resultant aspects of the environment and its inhabitants of Tuṣita arise as textual and semantic forms; thus, it is called "the Buddha’s teaching.

As for *vipaśyanā* (contemplation), the full term is *āyāra*; this is "reverse contemplation," meaning that the mind diligently contemplates that wondrous realm and moves toward it, hence it is called contemplation.
As for Maitreya, he is also called Maitreya; all previous traditions have been erroneous. Now, the correct Sanskrit pronunciation is *Maitreya*, which translates here as "The Compassionate One."
There are two meanings of "Maitreya" (*maitrī*):
first, it is derived from maternal compassion; second, it is based on one's own compassion.
The former refers to Maitrīnī, which is a feminine form; because he followed his mother’s clan name of *maitrī*, he was named Maitreya.

As stated in the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish*, fascicle 60: "From birth, he was endowed with the thirty-two marks; his body was the color of purple-gold, and his countenance was exceptionally outstanding."
The regent was filled with joy and summoned a physiognomist to examine him.
Once the master had seen his features, he praised his excellence all the more.
As he wished to establish a name for him, he inquired about the signs present at the time of his birth.
Manu replied,
"Her mother’s nature has always been ill-tempered, yet since she conceived this child, she has shown compassion for those in suffering and distress.
The physiognomist then divined:
"Because of this child," he established a name for him, naming him Maitreya.
Later, "Cí" (慈) was simply a transliteration of "Maitreya."
"Maitrī" is masculine in gender; it is the cultivation of loving-kindness by its very nature.
As the Sūtra says: "The Buddha said:
'In the past, in this Jambudvīpa, there was a great king named Dharmaruci, which in this language means "Dharma-Love. "
At that time, there was a Buddha named Puṣya.
A certain bhikṣu entered the samādhi of loving-kindness; his physical form was serene and tranquil, emitting light that shone brilliantly.
The king asked:
"What meditative concentration has brought this monk to such a state?
The Buddha said,
"He has entered the concentration of loving-kindness."
The king felt even greater joy and said,
"This concentration of loving-kindness is so truly sublime!
I shall practice it throughout my lives without ceasing."
At that time, King Dharmavatsa was none other than the present Maitreya;
because he first conceived the aspiration from then on, he has always been called Maitreya, and through long cultivation until his nature was perfected, the Buddha also refers to him as Maitreya.
"Maitreya, because both the paternal and maternal lineages of his brahmin clan possessed loving-kindness (*maitrī*), he was named Maitreya.
Furthermore, the *Vasumitra-sūtra* states: 'Ara-maitreya'—this is translated here as 'Maitreya' (the Loving One)."
"The phrasing has changed, yet the meaning does not contradict it.
Another interpretation states:
"A-lo" (A-ra) is simply "Ajita" (A-yi-duo).
"Ānanda" is his name, and "Maitreya" is his clan name.
Since both the name and the clan name are pronounced together, there is no contradiction.
As for the term "bodhisattva," in Sanskrit it is called *bodhisattva*, which here means "enlightened sentient being."
Because sentient beings who are pratyekabuddhas are the object [of the term], it is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.
Alternatively, because they are sentient beings capable of seeking great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*), it is a *bahuvrīhi* (dependent) compound.
What is now called "bodhisattva" is an abbreviation of speech.
Maitreya is himself a bodhisattva; thus, it is an *karmadhāraya* (attributive) compound.
Because he is the bodhisattva Maitreya, it is a *tatpuruṣa* (possessive) compound.

Regarding the term "born above" (*ūrdhva-janman*): "above" (*ūrdhva*) refers to ascending to a superior state, and "birth" (*janman*) refers to the arising of a new retribution. This means that by relying upon those superior celestial realms, various forms of retribution newly arise; this is one of the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*) of a Buddha’s life.
Regarding the Tuṣita Heaven, its full name is Doṣitā Deva; this is translated as the "Heaven of Contentment" (Zizu Tian), also known as the "Heaven of Joyful Contentment" (Xizu Tian).
This is because, while possessing sublime bliss in principle, they give rise to joy and contentment without sinking or floating.

Regarding the term "sūtra" (*sūtra*), it exists in its original form as *sūtranta*, which is translated here as "Scripture of Accordance" (*kīng*). This means that it accords with principle and accords with the capacities of sentient beings.

It accords with principle because it penetrates the meanings that ought to be taught; it accords with the capacities of beings because it sustains and gathers those sentient beings who are to be converted.

Therefore, the *Sphutārthā* states: "Because it pierces through and upholds the meanings that ought to be explained for the sake of sentient beings to be converted, it is called a *sūtra* (scripture).
This is stated in reference to the *Sūtra on Maitreya Bodhisattva’s Rebirth in Tuṣita Heaven*; thus, it is analyzed according to the *tatpuruṣa* (dependent determinative) compound.
Regarding the subsequent general explanation of the titles, there are briefly five gates:
first, the gate of the relative distinction between persons and dharmas; that is to say, "Buddha" and "Maitreya" are names for persons, while the remaining names refer to dharmas.
Second is the gate of the relative opposition between teaching and meaning: that is, the spoken word and the name of the sutra are called "teaching," while the remainder is called "meaning.
Third is the gate of the relative opposition between mind and object: that is, the contemplation of names is called "mind," while the remainder is called "object."

Fourth is the gate of the correspondence between primary and secondary retribution: this refers to Maitreya’s rebirth in the upper realm as the primary retribution (*vipāka*), and the Tuṣita Heaven as the secondary retribution (*niśraya*).

Fifth is the gate of the correspondence between the general and the specific: this means that the Buddha’s preaching of the sūtra is called "general" because it also applies to other sūtras, whereas the contemplation of Maitreya and so forth is called "specific" because it is restricted to this particular sūtra.
Fifth, regarding the word-by-word commentary, it is divided into two general sections:

the first sutra explains Maitreya’s ascent to heaven to propagate the teachings and bring benefit and joy; the latter two sutras explain Maitreya’s descent among humans to propagate the teachings and bring benefit and joy.

Although the manifested transformations of a Bodhisattva in his final birth (caramabhavika) consist of eight phases, they are briefly described as occurring only within the auspicious realms of humans and devas; therefore, the first section establishes the superior benefit and happiness for those above.

Now, regarding this initial sūtra, the divisions of the human realm differ: there may be three, four, five, six, or eighteen sections, as the number—whether many or few—is determined according to one's preference, and thus cannot be recorded in full.
Furthermore, according to the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, this sutra is divided into three parts:

first, the section on the causes and conditions for the arising of the teaching (*nidāna-vibhāga*). This means that it generally reveals what has been heard and the time when the teaching arose, and specifically reveals the teacher and the place where the teaching arose; the sentient beings for whom the teaching is intended are precisely the cause and the object-condition for the arising of the teaching.
Next is the section on what is taught in the sacred teachings (*āgama*), which means it correctly reveals the distinctions among the categories of dharma-gates taught in the sacred teachings.

Finally is the section on practicing according to the teachings, which means it reveals how the assembly at that time, having heard the Buddha’s sacred teachings, received them with joy and put them into practice.
The first two [sections] at the beginning are:
first, the *Saddharmapraśaṃsā-nidāna* (Testimony of Faith);
second, the *Utpatti-nidāna* (Originative Introduction). Master Wonhyo said:

"The Sūtra states: 'During the first watch of the night,' and so forth, which constitutes the introductory nidāna; this refers to the Tathāgata’s emission of light and the bestowal of predictions by the emanated Buddhas, as these are the causes for the arising of the teaching."
Master Ji said:

"The section beginning with 'Extending the broad and long tongue' constitutes the Prologue of the Exhortation (*nidāna*), because those for whom the teaching is intended constitute the Prologue of Certification and Faith (*śraddhā-prasāda-nidāna*)."
"No; for that would contradict the six and five categories (*padārtha*) of the various treatises.

Now, the previous explanation is preferable: although the capacity of the audience for whom the teaching is intended has already been established through faith, this present passage exists to manifest the characteristics [of the teaching]; therefore, it is appropriate to serve as its introduction.
If Master Ki says:
"According to ancient interpretations, there are six parts in the introduction;
however, according to the present *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, there are only five."
This is also not the case.

The emission of light, the rain of flowers, and the bestowal of predictions by transformation-buddhas are certainly not common to all sūtras; rather, this was stated because the *Buddhabhūmi-sūtra* itself explains its intended audience immediately after the section on the revealed teaching (*deśanā-dharma*).
One must not cite this example for all sūtras.
This [sūtra] consists of five sections; it should be stated that there are four in the introductory section (nidāna) of this sūtra, excluding the "object of the teaching" (vineya).
The phrase "Thus" refers to the words of those who transmit the Buddha’s teachings.
One should give rise to faith because such matters as these I have heard in the past.
Within this, there are four points:
First, reliance on analogies; second, reliance on instructions; third, reliance on questions and answers; fourth, reliance on permissions. Regarding "analogies":
the Dharma thus transmitted and heard is exactly as the Buddha taught it, without any difference, serving as the cause for skillful means to bring about benefit and happiness.
Regarding "relying on instruction," this refers to speech that is distant in being the instruction of the Buddha, or proximate in being the instruction of a transmitter of the Dharma.
Regarding "relying on question and answer," it means that someone asks:
"Did you previously hear what you have said?"
For this reason, he replied:
"Thus have I heard.
Regarding the basis of authorization, at the time of the compilation, the assembly of bodhisattvas collectively requested:
"As you have heard, so should you speak.
Thus, the transmitter of the Dharma granted permission, saying:
"As I have heard, so shall you speak."
Regarding this, one sutra states that it relies solely upon permission (*anujñā*), while another states it relies solely upon question and answer (*praśnottara*).
According to the true meaning, when a sutra says "thus" (*evam*), it applies universally to all four meanings.
The meaning may be understood by inference.
Regarding the phrase "Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*), the Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma refers to himself, saying:
"Such a Dharma as this was heard directly from the Buddha."
Therefore, it is called "I heard.

"I" refers to the conventional, provisional entity consisting of the aggregates (*skandhas*); "heard" refers to the ear-faculty giving rise to consciousness and the rational reception [of sound]. By subsuming the particular under the general, it is said: "I heard."
Question:
Since all teachings on the fundamental vows state that one must eliminate the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*), why is it not said that one hears [the Dharma] through "non-self" (*anātman*)?
Answer:
Regarding the four reasons for merely stating "as I have heard":
first, it is because the expression is easy to understand; that is to say, if one were to say "there is no self," it would not clarify what is being negated.
Second, it is because it accords with worldly convention; that is to say, the Tathāgata’s speech is never otherwise than true, as it is established by the common measure of sentient beings.
Third, to eliminate the fear of non-self: that is, if one says there is no self, for whose sake would one practice and train?
Fourth, because there exist the causal activities of defilement and purification pertaining to self and others; if one says there is no self, these distinctions could not be expressed.
Question:
If that is so, why does he not state his name, but instead say "I have heard"?
Answer:

There are three meanings. First, it does not contradict worldly convention; that is to say, in the Western Regions, people generally refer to themselves as "I. Although this school reveals the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), its teachings do not depart from the conventional; although its principles reveal the subtle, its expressions do not depart from the coarse. This is because it seeks to demonstrate that the ultimate truth is not separate from the conventional.

The second "I" signifies mastery and sovereignty; Ānanda was of great learning, retaining all that he heard, possessing both the words and their meanings, and upholding the Tripiṭaka, thereby attaining mastery over the teachings.
If one uses the term "self" (ātman) as a designation, although it conforms to correct reasoning, it lacks the sense of attaining mastery over all phenomena.
The third [meaning of] "self" is that of "intimacy," meaning that it is commonly spoken of in the world as "I see" or "I hear."
For these three reasons, it is said simply that "I heard" rather than "Ananda saw.
Question:
At that time, Ananda also saw and perceived what the Tathāgata spoke; why then does he not say "I saw and perceived"?
Answer:
There are also three reasons.

First, because one must first hear the teachings in order to realize the truth; second, because in this realm, the Buddha’s work is accomplished through sound; and third, because those who aspire to realize Bodhi must listen with a mind of profound respect.
The general term "transmission of the Dharma" is used so that sentient beings may be inspired to revere, believe in, and accept it.
Thus, by stating "I have heard this from the Buddha," one ensures that the words and meanings are definitive, without any addition or subtraction; therefore, it is said, "Thus have I heard."
Regarding the phrase "at one time" in the Sūtra, it refers to the time when the second teaching arose.

The Śāstra states: "Time is a conventional designation established upon conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*); that is, it is a conventional designation established upon various phenomena such as form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*), and is subsumed within the aggregate of formations dissociated from thought (*viprayuktasaṃskāraskandha*)."
In this context, there are two meanings.

First, the meaning of "time" according to logical principle (*yukti-kāla*): that is to say, because within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) of those present as speakers and listeners, there exists the sense of repaying what precedes and inducing what follows, the three times are provisionally established and collectively termed "one time."
Second, regarding the time of mere consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*): this refers to when the minds and consciousnesses of both the teacher and the audience retroactively construct the three times.
Question:
Since the times are distinct, why are four or six times and so forth not mentioned?
Answer:
Because the divisions of day and night are not fixed across all regions—that is, so that [the teaching] may circulate throughout all directions—it is explained as occurring over many periods.
Question:
Why not state specifically the duration of time following the completion of the realization of the Way?
Answer:

Although it may be spoken of according to the manifested marks of transformation, because the depth of understanding seen by ordinary beings and sages differs, their perceptions of near and far differ as well; therefore, it cannot be stated definitively.
Question:

Since there are distinctions between purity and impurity regarding the locus, and since the teaching is definitively established according to the capacities [of beings], it may also be understood differently by ordinary persons and sages at different times.
Why, then, would it be an indeterminate teaching?
Answer:

While the distinction between pure and impure states can be known through their respective bases, the duration of time is indefinite and cannot serve as a fixed standard; this is because it varies according to whether one's faculties are sharp or dull, and thus the time may be long or short without certainty.

Since Ānanda was born on the night the Buddha attained enlightenment, he did not enter the transmission until thirty years later; yet all the sūtras state "at one time" because, when he entered the transmission, he requested that [the teachings] be spoken again, and thus there is no error in them not being "at one time."
Question:
When further explaining, does one speak a single phrase or many aspects?
Answer:

By speaking a single phrase, because the faculty of hearing has attained mastery, one hears that single phrase and immediately understands immeasurable meanings, as explained at length in the *Baoen jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness).
Regarding the term “Buddha” in the Sūtra, this third section specifically clarifies the Teacher.

In the Sanskrit language it is called *buddha*, which here means “the Awakened One. This refers to one who has fully attained the two types of wisdom and permanently severed the two obstacles, thereby attaining self-awakening regarding all objects of experience.
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In Sanskrit it is called Bhagavān; this single name is used to collectively represent all his virtues.
The passage from the Sūtra beginning with "In the country of Śrāvastī" marks the fourth location where the teaching was given.
Paramārtha says:

"In the past, there were two brothers, one named Śāmba and the other named Bhadrika. They cultivated the Way on this mountain and attained the fruits [of the path]; thus, the city-state was named Śrāvastī."
Now, what is called the Brahma-voice city of Śrāvastī is the capital of the kingdom of Kośala within the region of Central India.
To distinguish it from Southern Kośala, the name of the capital city has been used as the name of the kingdom.

This is called the City of Abundant Virtue because it possesses four virtues: namely, first, the possession of material wealth; second, exquisite objects of desire; third, abundance of learning; and fourth, an abundance of liberation.
The ancient accounts stating that the people of this country were all "deluded" (or "corrupted") are erroneous.

This, rather, signifies the virtues manifested by Maitreya’s birth: namely, that material wealth and objects of desire constitute mundane virtue, while extensive learning and liberation constitute supramundane virtue.
"Ji" (祇) is the name of the Prince; in Sanskrit it is called Jetavana, which here means "Victorious Grove.
It is said that when the Prince was born, an enemy from a neighboring country arrived; he fought and achieved victory, and thus this became his name.
The name "Jeta" (Tree) reveals the name of the minister; in the Sanskrit language he was the elder Sudatta, which here means "Good Giver.

Because he practiced benevolent giving and was fit to relieve the poor and destitute and compassionately succor the orphaned and the aged, people at that time praised his virtue and called him Anāthapiṇḍada (Giver to the Destitute).
The ancient term "Ji-shu" (Jetavana) is a corruption.
The name of its king, formerly called "Bo-si-ni" (Prasenajit), is also a corruption.
According to current Sanskrit, he is called *Prasenajit*, which translates here as "Victorious Army."
Its grove is also called a *vihāra*; in China, it is termed a "temple" (*si*).
The *Śāstra* states: "The kingdom of Śrāvastī lies on the southern bank of the Ganges River; five *li* from the river, there is the Anāthapiṇḍada Garden."

This expresses Maitreya’s virtue of benefiting both self and others: namely, that the "Victorious Grove" (Jeta-vana) signifies his benefit for himself, because he has subdued the Māras through wisdom;
whereas the "Solitary Garden" (Ekārāma) signifies his entrustment to benefiting others, because he rescues sentient beings through compassion.
Regarding the term "location," the *Dīpa-śāstra* states: "There are two kinds:
first, the location of the mind; second, the location of the body.
As for the location of the body, examples include the Bamboo Grove Monastery (*Veṇuvana-vihāra*) and Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa-parvata*), and so forth."
There are six states in which that mind abides:
first, the Brahma-abodes, because it dwells in the four immeasurables;
second, the celestial abodes, because it dwells in the four dhyānas.
Third is the dwelling of the sages, because they dwell in supernormal powers (*abhijñā*).
Fourth is the dwelling of the life-span, because they dwell in the fivefold Dharma-body (*pañcāṅgika-dharmakāya*).
Fifth is the dwelling of deportment, because they dwell in the mind of the four modes of deportment (*īryāpatha*).
The six great abidings exist because they abide in the principle of the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*).
These six are precisely the abiding in the objective realm; they are the unique abiding of the Buddha, such that one cannot say the Buddha abides together with the bhikṣus.
"If the body abides, it is an abiding by way of dependence; thus, there can be the Buddha dwelling together with the bhikṣus.
The sūtra says, "At that time, during the first watch of the night," and so forth; this is the second introductory section on the occasion of the teaching.
This section has two parts:
first, manifesting signs to summon the assembly; second, proclaiming the Dharma to obtain benefits.
Within the first part, there are also two sub-sections:
First is the manifestation of signs to summon the assembly; second is the appearance of signs as the assembly gathers.
Within the first, there are three parts:
first, the summons by emitting light; second, the summons by raining down flowers; and third, the summons by bestowing predictions of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*).
This is the first [point].
Question:

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* says "at dawn," the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* says "during the day," and the *Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* says "at midday"; what is the meaning of this sūtra’s statement that it was "at the first watch of the night"?
Answer:

Because Śākyamuni appeared in an age of five turbidities, the classes of sentient beings he transformed were heavy [in their afflictions]. Therefore, those who had not yet been delivered were exceedingly ignorant; for this reason, he further illuminated during the first watch of the night and the last watch.
Another interpretation is as follows:

"The interval before the sun sets tomorrow" refers to the first watch of the night; this is a metaphor for the time when Śākyamuni has already entered *nirvāṇa* and Maitreya is about to manifest his traces.
"Pervading" (*ju*) means to be all-pervasive, specifically that it pervades throughout the body.
The "emission of light" signifies the Buddha’s compassion that universally rescues all beings.
Regarding the color of the light: the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* mentions white; the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* mentions four colors; and the preceding passage of this sūtra mentions ten billion colors.

Regarding the present mention of "golden clouds," this signifies the sense of being preeminent among treasures; that is to say, because they are the foremost treasure for benefiting beings in the final age.

Some say that the *ārāma* (park) is no different from the previous *ārāma*, and that what is now called the "park" refers to the Jetavana Vihāra, while the "house" refers to the residence of the elder.
The Sūtra states, "There was golden light," and so forth; this is the second section, the raining of flowers to summon [the assembly].
This means that the Buddha’s compassion is like a cloud, providing shade for the four modes of birth; therefore, he rains down flowers.
Question:
For what reason did the garden become [the property of] Sudatta, and why did the clouds illuminate the kingdom?
Answer:
Because "garden" (*ārāma*) signifies the sense of being encompassed on all sides, it is used as a metaphor for the seven circumambulations.
Because it destroys the seven types of wrong views and causes one to attain the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*), it is narrow.
Because the kingdom is vast and all those with whom there is a connection are covered by its grace, "cloud" (*megha*) serves as the metaphor.
Question:
The latter two sūtras do not summon the assembly; why, then, does this sūtra summon the assembly?
Answer:

Now it is said that when the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, there must necessarily be manifest signs to summon the assembly; however, as for those who compile the teachings, such signs may or may not exist.
As for the "lotus," the lotus possesses five virtues:
first, its ability to conceal, which is a metaphor for extinguishing all transgressions.
Second, its ability to produce fruit is a metaphor for hearing this sutra and seeing Maitreya Buddha to attain the fruit of the Way.
Third, its fragrance being heard from afar is a metaphor for studying this sutra so that the Buddha’s illustrious reputation is widely proclaimed.
Fourth, it can produce water, which is a metaphor for those who hear this sutra being born from the ocean of birth and death.
Fifth, it can cause blossoming, which is a metaphor for the present Buddha unfolding the subtle meanings for future Buddhas.

The first four virtues represent the benefits gained by sentient beings through their practice, while the final virtue represents Maitreya’s attainment of the fruit of omniscience (*sarvajñatā*) upon the completion of his causal path.
"Sublime meaning" refers to this omniscience.
The Sūtra states, "Within that radiance," and so forth; this is the third section, the Summons of the Prophecy.
This section has two parts:
first, the prophecy concerning the master, and second, the actual bestowal of the prophecy; these may be understood accordingly.
The "Transformation Buddha" (nirmāṇa-buddha) is so called because he manifests the event of Maitreya’s rebirth in the upper realm to entice those who do not yet realize that [the world] is not real;
thus, he is called a transformation buddha. Furthermore, because the spiritual transformations of all Buddhas are inconceivable, he is called "Great."
The Sūtra states: "They all uttered these words... up to Maitreya. This passage is briefly explained through six sections: first, the length of the kalpas; second, the number of Buddhas;

third, the sequence of generating the aspiration for enlightenment; fourth, the order and skipping of practices; fifth, the provisional and ultimate nature of the realization of the fruit; and sixth, a further explanation of the original text.

Regarding the length of the kalpas: it was formerly said that sixty-four kalpas constitute the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Aeon). Because the number sixty-four—derived from the cycles of fire, water, and so forth—is termed the "greatest kalpa," later masters have for the most part adopted this explanation, taking the Buddha as the measure of the Bhadrakalpa; that is, the appearance of one thousand Buddhas constitutes the full extent of the Bhadrakalpa.
The manifestation of the Buddhas is not fixed; therefore, Master Xuanzang said:
"The twenty kalpas of abiding are called the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Kalpa).
All masters in India maintain this view, and there is no further dispute."

However, the ninth fascicle of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "During the ninety kalpas preceding [the present], three Buddhas appeared in the world: in the first kalpa, Vipaśyin Buddha appeared;
in the thirty-second kalpa, two Buddhas appeared—the first named Śikhin and the second named Viśvabhū;

and in the ninety-first kalpa, one thousand Buddhas appeared. Specifically, at the beginning of that kalpa, four Buddhas appeared: the first named Krakucchanda, the second named Kanakamuni, the third named Kāśyapa, and the fourth named Śākyamuni."

Furthermore, regarding the statement in the *Lokaprajñapti* that among the twenty kalpas of the world's formation, Buddhas do not appear during the first five kalpas or the final ten kalpas, but appear only during the intermediate five kalpas, this is all explained according to the *anuvartana-naya* (the principle of conforming discourse).
Since their bases are different, they do not contradict one another.
Otherwise, it would contradict the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*, which states: "In immeasurable ages, there was a Buddha who appeared in the world named Amitābha."
Furthermore, according to the tradition of the Brahmins:
although this present intermediate kalpa (antarakalpa) is called the ninth kalpa in the Hīnayāna school, it is the first among the twenty *vāsakalpas* (abiding kalpas) according to the Mahāyāna.
Therefore, the Mahāyāna states that the four Buddhas beginning with Krakucchanda all appeared during the first kalpa, while the remaining Buddhas appeared during the subsequent nineteen kalpas.
Furthermore, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "In the first and last kalpas, there is likewise increase and decrease.
Thus, we know that it is not only during the period of decrease that Buddhas appear; there is no contradiction in Buddhas appearing even during the period of increase.
For this reason, during the first ten kalpas, nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas appear, while during the final ten kalpas, only the Buddha Ruci appears.

If one interprets it in this way, the *Sūtra on the Vajrapāṇi Good-Compliant One* states: "Ruci attains Buddhahood last; his lifespan is half a kalpa, and the number of beings he delivers is equal to that of the nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas, without any distinction."

Among the three explanations, the latter is superior; otherwise, how could the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* state: "The devaputras of the Śuddhāvāsa heavens see the lotus when the kalpa is forming, and thereby know that there shall be one thousand Buddhas in the Bhadrakalpa"?
Furthermore, the *Bodhisattva-tsaie-king* (The Sutra on the Bodhisattva Dwelling in the Womb) states: "When the Brahmā King has passed beyond the Bhadrakalpa, his life span shall come to an end.

Since this Bhadrakalpa consists of twenty intermediate kalpas (*antarakalpa*), by analogy, the two other kalpas—the past and the future—should likewise each consist of twenty intermediate kalpas. Thus, it should be explained that there are twenty kalpas:
those of formation are called the *Vibhūṣaṇakalpa* (Adornment Kalpa), and those of destruction are called the *Tārakakalpa* (Star Kalpa).
This means that since there are sentient beings during the periods of formation and destruction, Buddhas may appear to teach and transform them.

Regarding the second point—the greater or lesser number of Buddhas who appear—it is taught differently across various traditions concerning the appearance of Buddhas during the Bhadrakalpa (Auspicious Eon).
As the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "In the distant past, there was a Buddha named Anantavīrya.
At that time, there was a king named Puṣpaka; this king had a thousand sons, who were none other than the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa."
The *Vajrapāṇi-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a wheel-turning monarch who had a thousand sons; each of them gave rise to the bodhicitta and vowed to seek buddhahood."
The commentary explains:
This is likely King Puṣpavanta.
The *Bhaiṣajyarāja-bhaiṣajyasamudgata-sūtra* also speaks in this same way.

The *Karunapundarika Sutra* states: "During the latter half of the Bhadrakalpa, one thousand and four bodhisattvas shall attain unsurpassed enlightenment; thereafter, in the subsequent kalpa, the Tathagata Ruci shall preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings."
Therefore, the sixth fascicle of that sutra states: "The Brahma-king Ratnasāgara addressed the Buddha Ratnagarbha, saying:
'In the future world, during the Bhadrakalpa, how many Buddhas will appear in the world?'"
The Buddha said,
"In the half-aeon of Bhadra, one thousand and four Buddhas will appear in the world.
Ratnasāgara replied:
“World-Honored One!

After all the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa have entered parinirvāṇa, the dragon Varaprabha will finally attain unsurpassed enlightenment, named Nārāyaṇapratibhānabhaiṣajya, and he will appear in the world during the latter half of a kalpa.”

"After the parinirvāṇa of all Buddhas and the subsequent extinction of their True Dharma, I shall then attain unexcelled enlightenment; my lifespan shall be equal to that obtained by the fourteen thousand Buddhas, and my śrāvaka disciples shall likewise be so, without any difference."
"If, after my parinirvāṇa, the True Dharma and the Bhadrakalpa were to perish simultaneously," the Buddha Ratnagarbha said, "In a future age,

after one asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges has passed, and during the latter part of a second asaṃkhyeya kalpa equal to the sands of the Ganges, fourteen buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa will attain unexcelled enlightenment."

"You shall receive offerings of food and drink, attain unsurpassed enlightenment, and be named Loushi; your lifespan shall be half a kalpa, and your śrāvaka disciples shall be no different from those of the fourteen thousand Buddhas."
The commentary states:
Based on this textual evidence, it is clearly understood that there are one thousand five hundred Buddhas in the Bhadrakalpa.
Question:
Question: For what reason do other sutras mostly speak of the thousand Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa, while the *Karunapundarika Sutra* speaks of fifteen hundred Buddhas?
Answer:
Some say it is because their perceptions of sentient beings' capacities differ.
Some say that when other sutras speak of "a thousand Buddhas," they do so according to a general approximation, such as the measurement of Mount Sumeru.
However, it is said that in reality there are one thousand five hundred Buddhas in the Bhadrakalpa.

Yet, because the aforementioned three sutras discuss the simultaneous generation of the aspiration for enlightenment (*cittotpāda*) and the sequential attainment of Buddhahood, they refer only to a thousand Buddhas; this refers to the *Suvarṇaprabhāsa-sūtra* (or *Kinnararāja-paripṛcchā*), in which each of the thousand sons individually generates the aspiration for enlightenment.
Question:
The *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* states: "From the Buddha Kanakacchanda up to the ninth hundred and ninety-ninth Buddha, together they constitute one great kalpa."
"From the first thousand stories up to the Buddha, it takes a single kalpa alone.
The *Loutan jing* (Lokadhātu-sūtra) is also like this.
That sūtra asks: "By what measure is one great kalpa defined?"
Answer:
Some say that eighty kalpas constitute one great kalpa; that is, forty kalpas of the empty eon during which no Buddha appears, followed by [the subsequent period], are collectively termed one kalpa.
Question:
How is it known that a Buddha appears during the kalpa of destruction?
Answer:
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "After the parinirvāṇa of the Buddha Lokeśvararāja, the True Dharma and the Bhadrakalpa will simultaneously perish.
Since it says that the True Dharma and the Bhadrakalpa perish at the same time, we know that the Buddha appears during the kalpa of destruction (*saṃvartakalpa*).

Some say this is not so, because Buddhas appear during the period of kalpa-decrease according to various treatises, and because there is no stage of decrease during either the kalpa of formation or the kalpa of destruction; therefore, one should state that twenty intermediate kalpas constitute one great kalpa.

Others say the same: if it is argued that a Buddha appears during a period of decline and this treatise serves as proof, since the Buddha does not appear after that treatise has declined for one hundred years, then Lohita Buddha—who remains for twenty kalpas—should be said to have lived during the time of nine hundred and ninety-nine Buddhas, with their periods of increase and decrease equaling one and a half kalpas. Therefore, Lohita Buddha also lasts for half a kalpa, because his lifespan is equal to that of all other Buddhas.
Question:
How is it known that the appearance of the Buddhas in the world lasts for only half an eon?
Answer:
Although this is not explicitly stated in the fixed text, by analogy it must be so.

Furthermore, another interpretation is that the various Buddhas of the past appeared during the first ten kalpas, while the final Buddha, Ruci, appears in the eleventh kalpa; thus, the remaining nine kalpas are all covered by the legacy of Ruci’s Dharma.
If one were to say that ten kalpas constitute one kalpa, and that the subsequent ten kalpas are referred to as half a kalpa, there would be no error in meaning.
Regarding the sequence of the third production of the thought of enlightenment: Question:
Between Śākyamuni and Maitreya, who first produced the thought of enlightenment?
Answer:
Maitreya was first, and Śākyamuni was later.
Therefore, the *Buddhapiṭaka Sūtra* states: "Forty kalpas after Maitreya had generated the aspiration for enlightenment, Śākyamuni then generated the aspiration."

Furthermore, the *Maitreya-bodhisattva-pūrvapraṇidhāna-sūtra* states: "Maitreya Bodhisattva conceived the aspiration for enlightenment forty-two kalpas before me; I subsequently conceived the aspiration for the Way."
"In this Bhadrakalpa, through great diligence, he transcended nine kalpas to achieve perfect enlightenment.

Furthermore, the *Buddhacarita-sūtra* states: "In the past, there was a Tathāgata named Suvicintita; it was at the place of that Buddha that Maitreya Bodhisattva first resolved his mind [on enlightenment]."
Maitreya Bodhisattva awakened to the bodhicitta more than forty kalpas before me; only then did I awaken to the mind of the Way.
In the past, there was a Buddha named Sihaṃdhara Tathāgata; at that Buddha’s land, I was a king of scholars named Laoshan, and it was there that I first awakened the mind.
"In all these various sutras, it is stated that Maitreya first resolved his mind [for enlightenment] and Śākyamuni resolved his mind later.
Question:

"If this is so, why does the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* praise the Buddha’s diligence, stating that Śākyamuni Buddha and Maitreya and the other bodhisattvas resolved their minds simultaneously, yet the power of Śākyamuni’s diligence transcended nine *kalpas*?"
Answer:
These two bodhisattvas have two ways of generating the resolve: first, the definitive; second, the non-definitive.
Those with non-definitive resolve generate it simultaneously.
If one speaks of the resolute mind itself, it possesses its own sequence of before and after.
According to the full exposition of the principles, one should state this:
Bodhisattva Maitreya produced the resolute mind more than forty kalpas ago, and only thereafter did Śākyamuni produce the resolute mind.
However, by the power of their diligence, they transcended more than forty intermediate kalpas and attained enlightenment together within the same kalpa.
Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā* states: "There are those who first generated an undetermined mind and later generated a resolute mind, such as the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni and others."
"This means that the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni gave rise to the resolute mind because of Śākyamuni Buddha, and the Bodhisattva Maitreya gave rise to the resolute mind because of Maitreya Buddha.
Question:

"If the Bodhisattva Śākyamuni gave rise to his mind without doubt because of Śākyamuni Buddha, for what reason did he obtain the cause for Maitreya to give rise to his mind because of Maitreya Buddha?"
Answer:

The *Sarvajñāprabhasya-ṛṣi-maitracitta-sūtra* states: "The Buddha was staying at the monastery of the Īśvaradeva Temple in the village of Mṛgāramātṛ near the site of enlightenment in the kingdom of Magadha."
At one time, the Buddha was walking in meditation within a grove together with twelve hundred and fifty bhikṣus.
The Bodhisattva Maitreya, possessing a golden complexion and excellent marks, emitted silver light; adorned with gold like a mountain of white silver, he approached the place where the Buddha was.
Five hundred *brahmacārin* with matted hair saw Maitreya from afar; prostrating themselves with their five limbs touching the ground, they addressed the Buddha with this inquiry:
"The radiance of Maitreya is equal to that of the Buddha."
"Under which Buddha did you first resolve to attain the Way?
The Buddha told the brahmin:

"In the distant past, immeasurable, boundless, and incalculable *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas ago, there was a world named Supuṣpita, where the Buddha was named Maitreya; he constantly taught and transformed beings through the four immeasurable states of mind, beginning with loving-kindness."
At that time, there was a great Brahmin named Sarvajñāprabha who, though he gave rise to challenges and objections, could not be defeated. He then conceived faith and made this vow:
"May I uphold the sutras spoken by that Buddha and surely attain Buddhahood under the name Maitreya."
At that time, the brahmin entered a mountain valley and spent eight thousand years begging for food and reciting the sūtras.
Then, malevolent stars appeared out of season and the floods did not cease, so that he was unable to beg for food for seven days.
At that time, there were five hundred white hares in that forest, among whom was a hare king and his mate. Seeing the seer without food, they spoke these words:
"The seer has not eaten for many days for the sake of the Dharma; the mountain of Dharma is about to collapse, and the ocean of Dharma is about to dry up."
"I should not begrudge my life for the sake of the Dharma now.
He then addressed the rabbits:
"All conditioned phenomena are impermanent."
"Sentient beings cherish their own bodies and have never done so for the sake of the Dharma.
Then he spoke in verse:
"If there are those of the animal realm Who hear the names of the Buddhas..."
Forever departing from the three evil realms, Not being born in the eight difficult states;
If one hears the Dharma and practices it accordingly, One will always encounter a Buddha wherever one is born.
Believing in the Dharma without doubt, Taking refuge in the noble Sangha.
"By following all the precepts and practices, one will thus swiftly attain Buddhahood,
surely reach Great Nirvana, and constantly enjoy unsurpassed bliss.
He then addressed the rabbits, saying:
"I now wish to make offerings to the Dharma with my own body;
may you all rejoice in this.
For many kalpas, driven by the three poisons, I have taken the forms of birds and beasts, undergoing birth and death in vain."
She said to her son,
"You may seek out water and grass as you please, but maintain right mindfulness of the Triple Gem.
Hearing his mother's instruction, the son said to her:
"If one performs the offering of the Dharma, I too shall rejoice in it.
Following his mother, he entered the fire.
When the Bodhisattva relinquished his body, heaven and earth shook, and the heavens rained down flowers as an offering.
After the meat was cooked, the tree deities addressed the seer, saying:
"The king of hares and his mother have cast their bodies into the fire for the sake of making an offering to the Dharma.
Now that the meat is cooked, you may certainly eat it."
Upon hearing the divine words, the seer was overcome with grief and unable to respond, yet he spoke this verse:
"Better to burn one's own body and destroy one's eyes than to bear to commit killing and eat living beings."
The Buddhas have taught the Sūtra of Compassion; within that sūtra it is said to practice compassion:
"One would rather break through one's own marrow and extract the brain than bear to eat the flesh of sentient beings."
"Having spoken these words, he threw himself into the fire pit and perished together with the rabbit.
The earth shook and the heavens trembled; by his supernatural power, the trees emitted light, and golden and white radiance shone forth, illuminating a thousand lands."

When the sentient beings saw the light, they immediately came to the site; seeing that the immortal and the rabbit had both perished in the fire, and having received the verses and the Buddhist sūtras he had spoken, they carried them back to the king. The king issued a proclamation, and all of them gave rise to the great bodhicitta.
The Buddha told the brahmin:
"The king of the rabbits at that time was my own self in this present life.
That rabbit's cub was Rāhula."
The seer who recited the sutras is now Maitreya;
the five hundred hares are the five hundred disciples such as Mahākāśyapa;
and the mountain tree deity is Śāriputra, Maudgalyāyana, and the other two hundred and fifty disciples.
The thousand kings of those lands at that time were none other than the present thousand bodhisattvas, such as Bhadrapāla and the others.
Those sentient beings of that country who heard this sutra are those who shall attain the Way under the Buddhas of the Bhadrakalpa.
"By this, it is known with certainty that he first encountered Maitreya Buddha and gave rise to the resolute mind; therefore, he is named Maitreya.
However, because the *Sūtra of the Wise and the Foolish* refers to his later stage, it speaks of the time of Puṣya Buddha."
Regarding the fourth stage of practice, "Successive Transcendence":
Question—Since Maitreya first generated the aspiration for enlightenment and Śākyamuni did so later, why was it that at the time of attaining Buddhahood, Śākyamuni attained it first?
Answer:
Because neither the sūtras nor the śāstras clarify this, the oral traditions have not been consistent.
Master Ji says:
"It was more than forty *kalpas* ago that Śākyamuni first resolved to attain enlightenment.

However, the third fascicle of the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*, in the chapter "Resolving to Make Offerings," states: "In the past, there appeared a Buddha named Puṣya; seeing that Buddha, joy arose in my heart, and with palms joined and one foot raised, I praised that Buddha for seven days and seven nights."
The Buddha said,
"This person shall become a Buddha after ninety-four kalpas.
The Buddha Jiantili said:
"This person shall attain Buddhahood after ninety-three kalpas," said [the Buddha].
Vipaśyin Buddha said:
"This person shall attain Buddhahood after ninety kalpas."
The *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra*, fascicle seven, states: "By serving Buddha Puṣya, he stood on one foot and offered praise; therefore, he transcended nine kalpas.
The *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* says: "The Bodhisattva of the Snowy Mountains sacrificed his body for the sake of half a verse, thereby transcending twelve kalpas."
The *Suvarṇaprabhāsa Sūtra* states: "When Prince Sattva cast himself down, he transcended eleven kalpas.
Furthermore, when the rishi Maṇava spread his hair, he transcended eight kalpas."
Among these various types of skipping [kalpas], if one skips nine kalpas, it occurs during the period of cultivating the karma for the marks and signs over one hundred kalpas.
As for the remaining instances of skipping, they all occur within the three *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas* according to their respective circumstances.
If it were not so, at what stage could one further speak of "leaping over"?
Master Qin said:

"Regarding the leap of nine *kalpas* by praising Buddha Puṣya for seven days and seven nights—this occurred when the third *asaṃkhyeya-kalpa* was nearing completion; the karma for his marks and signs required exactly ninety-one *kalpas* to reach full perfection."
Therefore, all those who transcend kalpas during their various stages do so within the three great asaṃkhyeya kalpas.
Taking the transgressions before and after together, they transcend forty kalpas.
At the time of attaining fruition, they will be in the same kalpa as Maitreya Buddha.
Question:
How is it known that Puṣya Buddha was the last [Buddha] of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa?
Answer:

According to the *Buddhacarita-sūtra*: "After the Buddha Puṣya, there were four great kalpas; during the first of these great kalpas, there was only the Buddha Puṣya, who gave Śākyamuni the prophecy: 'In the future, after ninety-four kalpas, you shall become a Buddha.'"
"In the next great kalpa, there was only the Buddha Tattvadarśin, who prophesied, saying: 'In ninety-three future kalpas, you shall become a buddha.
In the final great kalpa, the Buddha Vipaśyin prophesied, saying: 'In ninety-one future kalpas, you shall attain buddhahood.'"
"In the third great kalpa, no Buddha was born at all because [Vipaśyin] had not yet received a prediction.
From this it is known that Vipaśyin Buddha was the final Buddha of the third asaṃkhyeya-kalpa.
Question:

If it was while [the Bodhisattva] was in the stage of the *saṃghāṭī* (a monk’s robe) when he saw Buddha Puṣya, how can it be said that by praising Buddha Puṣya, he surpassed nine *kalpas* in the cultivation of the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*)?
Answer:
This is a treatise in which the temporal divisions have been condensed and integrated.
Master Wenbei said:

"The Bodhisattva Śākyamuni subsequently resolved his mind [for enlightenment], yet when he encountered his original teacher Śākyamuni, he had already bypassed nineteen *kalpas*. At the time he was the youth on the Snowy Mountains (*Himavat*), he bypassed twelve *kalpas*; at the time he praised Buddha Puṣya, he bypassed nine *kalpas*. When he realized the fruit [of Arhatship], he attained the Way in the same *kalpa* as Maitreya."
The citations and textual interpretations all follow the explanation of the Qin dynasty.
Although there are these three explanations, none of them fully captures the underlying principle.
What error, then, could the Master Ji have committed?
The sūtras both state that he threw his body before a starving tigress, yet they do not mention that he thereby transcended eleven kalpas.
Furthermore, when the seer Maṇava spread out his hair, they merely say he received a prediction (vyākaraṇa), but do not say he transcended eight kalpas.
Therefore, both of these two explanations are devoid of any valid basis for their meaning;
because they transcend the facts, they are nothing but empty words.
What fault is there in the Qin interpretation?
Furthermore, it is said that after the Buddha Puṣya, there were four great kalpas during which Buddhas appeared in the world, yet no Buddha was born during the third kalpa.

If this is indeed the case, and since it is stated that after the passing of the Buddha Kiṃśuka one again encounters the Buddha Satyadarśin, how can it be said that the Buddha Puṣya was the final Buddha of the third asaṃkhyeya kalpa?
The final words of the Buddha must signify that there is no further [Buddha] after him.
Furthermore, the *Pitāputrasamāgama-śāstra* states: "Vipaśyin Buddha was the first Buddha after one hundred great kalpas; subsequently, Puṣya Buddha was mentioned."
